To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the use of a long-stem uncemented implant in a patient with a champagne flute femur can lead to a complication during broaching.
a femoral broach can get caught in the narrow diaphyseal canal of a champagne flute femur and that this can be managed via a longitudinal split of the femur.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of an innovative and reliable surgical technique for the removal of a broach that is stuck in a femoral canal.
the development of an innovative, minimally invasive, and cost-efficient surgical procedure for the treatment of femoral fractures in the elderly.
the development of a new type of femoral stem for uncemented total joint replacements in the hip.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
this case report describes a case of femoral canal broach complication in a patient with ‘champagneglass’ femur.
the use of long-stemmed implants is not recommended in cases of ‘champagne-flute’ femurs.
the surgeon must be very cautious when using a large broach in a patient with a relatively narrow femoral canal.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
a femoral component can be press fitted into the proximal femur, even when the distal tip is caught in the canal.
in cases of a narrow femoral diaphysis, a distal incision can be used to loosen a stuck femoral component during broaching.
the broaching technique is an essential component for successful uncemented primary hip arthroplasties.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the broach can be removed by opening up the distal femoral canal and that the longitudinal split of the femoral diaphysis can be secured with cables.
in patients with a narrow femoral diaphysis, a femoral broach may get stuck in the femoral canal and may not be removed with conventional techniques.
in patients with champagne flute femurs, the distal part of a broach can get stuck in the narrow canal during femoral broading.
